title: Theo and the Kitchen
premise: Marguerite Voss built her career orchestrating other people's perfect days while quietly grieving the wedding that never happened — hers, called off in a kitchen fire that nearly killed her. When a community festival's anonymous pen-pal program misfiles her letters to Theo Marchetti, the rival planner she blames for poaching clients, neither realizes at first who is on the other end, and both find themselves confessing things they've never said aloud. As the festival approaches and their identities surface mid-correspondence, Marguerite must choose between the armored life she survived into and the whole-hearted one Theo offers, culminating on the festival's final night when she finally steps back into a kitchen — not to survive it, but to belong in it.
about_author: Ansel Yarrow is the pen name of a former catering manager who spent a decade watching love arrive through service doors and loading docks. They write romance for people who believe tenderness is a discipline, not an accident.

chapters.title: The Vendor List
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She runs a flawless engagement-party walkthrough while privately cataloguing everything wrong with marriage, then learns the town festival committee has enrolled all local businesses in an anonymous pen-pal exchange. Beat: competent exterior, hollow interior.

chapters.title: Dear Stranger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He writes his first letter as a joke, complaining about a client who wants swans, and is startled when the reply is funnier and sharper than anything he expected. Beat: reluctant curiosity.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. In person, Marguerite and Theo spar over a shared venue booking; on paper, their aliases grow intimate. The dramatic irony tightens as each quotes the other's own words back unknowingly. Beat: doubling.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, flashback woven through present. The kitchen fire three years ago: the burned hand, the canceled wedding, the fiancé who couldn't look at her scars. She tells her pen pal none of this, but almost does. Beat: buried grief stirring.

chapters.title: Swans Are a Liability
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. His letter-writing becomes the best part of his week; he notices he's rescheduling site visits to check the mailbox. Meanwhile Marguerite outbids him for a marquee supplier, reigniting the rivalry. Beat: warmth undercut by competition.

chapters.title: The Committee Error
chapters.summary: Festival organizer Dot's POV (brief) reveals the misfiling: two enemies were paired deliberately by a volunteer who thought it was funny. Neither writer knows. Beat: ticking clock installed.

chapters.title: Lent Pieces
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her alias admits she 'lends pieces of herself and invoices for the privilege.' Theo reads it at his sister's kitchen table and recognizes the phrasing from a lost bid meeting. Beat: first suspicion.

chapters.title: A Test in Three Courses
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He plants a false detail in a letter; Marguerite's next business email echoes it back. He confirms her identity — and says nothing, ashamed of how much he wants to keep reading. Beat: complicity begins.

chapters.title: Rain on the Marquee
chapters.summary: Both POV, alternating scenes. A storm collapses the festival tent they're co-managing; soaked and laughing under a tarp, they have their first honest conversation without knowing what the other already knows. Beat: proximity.

chapters.title: The Scar Question
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her pen pal asks, gently, why she flinches around open flames at catered events. She writes four drafts and sends the truest one. Beat: confession by proxy.

chapters.title: What I Didn't Say at the Altar
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He confesses his own failure: a brother he didn't call back, a business built to avoid ever needing anyone. Marguerite reads it twice and cries in her car. Beat: mutual exposure.

chapters.title: Dot's Little Joke
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Dot, delighted with herself, lets slip that the pairing wasn't random. Marguerite works backward through every letter and lands on Theo's name with horror and something worse than horror. Beat: revelation.

chapters.title: Reading Him Backward
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She rereads the correspondence as Theo, hearing his voice in every line, furious that the tenderness was real and hidden. She stops answering. Beat: withdrawal.

chapters.title: Silence, Annotated
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Her silence tells him she knows. He drafts confessions he can't send, then shows up at her office instead and says it aloud: he knew for weeks and kept reading because it was the truest thing he'd ever been given. Beat: confrontation.

chapters.title: Everything I Wrote Was True
chapters.summary: Two-scene chapter, both POVs. Marguerite throws his betrayal of privacy at him; he refuses to apologize for meaning it. She orders him out — then can't throw away his last letter. Beat: rupture without resolution.

chapters.title: The Festival Roster
chapters.summary: Ensemble-tilted chapter, Marguerite's POV. Festival prep accelerates; forced collaboration means working side by side in charged silence while the whole town watches them not-speak. Beat: public pressure cooker.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Recipe Box
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Sorting her late mother's kitchen, she finds a recipe card annotated 'for when you stop being afraid of your own house.' She photographs it and, hands shaking, mails it to Theo unsigned. Beat: olive branch.

chapters.title: Answering the Card
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He cooks the recipe badly, photographs the disaster, and delivers the printout to her door with one line: 'Come teach me before the festival ends.' Beat: invitation.

chapters.title: The Kitchen
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, the emotional climax. She enters a working kitchen for the first time since the fire; panic rises, Theo doesn't rescue her but stays beside her, and she finishes the dish herself. She says yes — to him, to trying, to the whole heart. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: Sabotage at the Gate
chapters.summary: Both POV. A rival vendor's double-booking threatens to collapse the festival's final night; Marguerite and Theo work the crisis as a seamless unit, publicly, in front of everyone who bet against them. Beat: external climax mirroring internal repair.

chapters.title: Last Night of the Festival
chapters.summary: Alternating POV converging on one scene. Under string lights, Dot publicly takes credit for the pairing; Theo asks Marguerite for a first date like a man asking for a lifetime. She gives him the answer she once lent in pieces. Beat: payoff.

chapters.title: For When You Stop Being Afraid
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, epilogue-flavored. Months later, she plans a wedding again — small, imperfect, real — and Theo waits at a kitchen table set for two. Final line returns to the recipe card. Beat: belonging earned.
